t.2.54.1: Then Kausalyā, trembling again and again as if possessed by a spirit, lying on the ground as though lifeless, spoke to the charioteer.
t.2.54.2: Take me to where Kākutstha is, where Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa are; without them I cannot bear to live here even for a moment.
t.2.54.3: Turn the chariot back quickly and take me too to the Daṇḍakas; if I do not follow them, I shall go to the abode of Yama.
t.2.54.4: With a voice choked by a surge of tears and faltering, the charioteer, his palms joined in reverence, spoke these words, consoling the queen.
t.2.54.5: Cast off your grief and your bewilderment, and likewise the agitation born of sorrow; shaking off his anguish, Rāghava will dwell in the forest.
t.2.54.6: And Lakṣmaṇa too, knower of dharma and master of his senses, serving the feet of Rāma in the forest, wins for himself the world beyond.
t.2.54.7: Even in the lonely forest, Sītā, having found a dwelling as if in her own home, attains confidence and is unafraid, her heart entrusted to Rāma.
t.2.54.8: I do not notice in her any despondency at all, not even the slightest trace; Vaidehī appears to me as though she were accustomed to life in exile.
t.2.54.9: Just as Sītā used to delight in former days on going to the gardens of the city, so too does she delight even in the desolate forests.
t.2.54.10: Sītā, whose face is like the crescent moon, takes delight like a young girl; for that lovely woman, her heart wholly devoted to Rāma, is content even in the desolate forest.
t.2.54.11: For her heart has gone to him, and her very life depends on him; to her even Ayodhyā, bereft of Rāma, would be like a forest.
t.2.54.12: On the road Vaidehī asks about the villages and the towns, and, having seen the course of the rivers, about the many kinds of trees as well.
t.2.54.13: Neither the long journey, nor the force of the wind, nor distress, nor the heat of the sun can make the radiance of Vaidehī fade, for it is like the rays of the moon.
t.2.54.14: The face of the generous Vaidehī, resembling a lotus and shining with a radiance like that of the full moon, does not tremble.
t.2.54.15: Even now her feet, though bare of red lac-dye, appear as red as if stained with lac, shining with the radiance of a lotus bud.
t.2.54.16: Even now the lovely Vaidehī, though she has laid aside her ornaments, walks along playfully with that same delight, as though her graceful sport were still proclaimed by the jingling of her anklets.
t.2.54.17: Having taken refuge in the forest, she does not give way to fear when she sees an elephant, a lion or a tiger, for she relies on the arms of Rāma.
t.2.54.18: They are not to be grieved for, nor should you grieve for yourself, nor for the lord of the people; for this deed will stand firm in the world forever.
t.2.54.19: Shaking off their grief, with joyful hearts, firmly set upon the path trodden by the great sages, delighting in the forest and eating wild fruits, they faithfully keep their father's auspicious promise.
t.2.54.20: Even so, though the charioteer, speaking most fittingly, tried to restrain her, the queen, wasted by grief for her son, did not cease her wailing, crying "O beloved!", "O son!" and "O Rāghava!"
